doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Girls in school bands, Diva as role model, building new artists
summary: Many school bands are mostly girls though few see jazz as a career; Diva inspires them, and the industry won't invest in new artists.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Oh when you go to these high school competitions now, it’s very common to see more girl saxophone players than guys in the sections. My own daughter plays trumpet. She’s not by herself back there all the time either.

We were recently in Iowa and Leisl [Sagartz] and I went ahead of time to adjudicate a high school festival, there was like twenty bands. Most of them were girls, like in every band, almost every, like one band had one boy playing tenor, all girls.

Yeah. But women somehow still, the young girls don’t take it seriously. It’s very rare still I think that somebody says I think I’ll make jazz my career and go off and study. It still doesn’t seem like an option that’s really open for women. For some reason it’s just not even laid out in front of them. Sure you can do this, you can do that, you can do this, or be a jazz musician. Like very common. But I think one thing that Diva does which is great is certainly role models for the young women that if they want to take it seriously that yes there is hope, and a second thing is for any students, we’re the only big band that a lot of kids have ever seen live. And it’s incredible that they just barrel to the stage, and colleges too. The kids say, “we never saw a big band before.” And so they don’t care if we’re men, women or Martians, they’re just are so excited that it’s a big band and they never heard this kind of a sound live, you know, to me it’s so sad because it is expensive to move a big band but it’s really not as prohibitive as certainly not any Rock bands, but then you’re of course dealing with the drawing power. Or even an artist like the heavy hitting jazz stars which command fortunes and fortunes of money for trios and things like that. But — it’s well deserved but it’s just too bad that some of it really seems impossibly difficult to be building new artists. And it trickles down from the media to the record companies to the agents who Stanley our manager deals with, but me once in a while and through Stanley is nobody seems to have any desire in like building a new artist up. It’s like, “we’ll give you a record deal but you have to be famous first” kind of thing. Like, “we’ll book you on a tour but you have to have gigs first.” Like some bizarre — you have to prove to us that you have a tour already then we’ll book you on a tour. Like some bizarre — nobody’s willing to invest in — that’s one thing that I learned from Stanley that it’s the music business and the business part of any business, new business, is you have to invest in it. And he’s — I mean you have to. There’s so many new bands. In New York alone you can go on any given day you can go to probably ten big band rehearsals somewhere and hear some great music and some awful music. Some great music with some phenomenal players. And they go here’s my band, and then they don’t realize all the stuff that you’re going to have to pay for once things get rolling. They just think I formed a big band, here’s my ten charts, send me on a tour. And then they might very well deserve but it’s hard, a hard business.
